items.title: The Jet That Always Shadows Air Force One When The President Travels Abroad
items.summary:
U.S. President Donald Trump’s recent visit to China has drawn particular attention from online flight trackers. This is in no small part due to the fact that all three of the U.S. Air Force’s current Boeing 747-based Air Force One aircraft – the two older VC-25As and the new ex-Qatari VC-25B “Bridge” jet – have supported the trip. Another militarized 747, an E-4B Nightwatch , commonly referred to as a ‘doomsday plane,’ was also spotted shadowing the group to and from Asia. 

While this drew a lot of attention online, including blog posts from defense-focused sites, the reality is this is absolutely standard practice. The E-4B is just another part, albeit a very unique and shy one, of the massive aerial logistics ballet that occurs whenever the President leaves the country.

The Air Force currently has four E-4Bs, also known as National Airborne Operations Centers (NAOC), all based at Offutt Air Force Base in Nebraska. Based on the 747-200 model, three of these planes first entered service in the 1970s as E-4A Advanced Airborne Command Posts (AACP). Those aircraft were subsequently brought up to the E-4B NAOC standard in the 1980s, and were eventually joined by a fourth example converted straight to that configuration. The jets have been continuously upgraded over the years. In addition to supporting presidential travel, the Nightwatch aircraft also regularly transport the Secretary of Defense (now also referred to as the Secretary of War) and their staff during overseas trips, among other roles.

items.title: Congress, you can declare that sexual assault has no place in the military. Here’s how.
items.summary:
When you volunteer for military service, are you volunteering to be sexually assaulted? Far too often, the answer is yes – although few young men and women have that in mind when they imagine putting on the uniform. 

Adding insult to injury, under current law for the military, our service members can’t take anyone in the military to court for the assault. Congress has an opportunity to change that in this lame-duck session. They must not waste this chance.

We all know that sexual assault has long plagued the military. You might remember the Tailhook scandal, or the crimes at the Aberdeen Proving Ground, or the dozens of trainees assaulted by instructors at Lackland Air Force Base, or the horrific murder of Vanessa Guillen by a fellow soldier at Ford Hood. The military’s independent investigation after that killing found a “ permissive environment ” for sexual assault and sexual harassment at Fort Hood – nearly thirty years after leaders vowed they would root out sexual violence in the military.

Every time one of these comes to light, leadership makes some changes — a new hotline , new procedures for prosecuting sex crimes, new data collection approaches. But the assaults continue. 

The Pentagon estimates that last year, some 20,000 active-duty service members were sexually assaulted out of a total of 1.3 million. The actual number is probably far higher. items.t: Congress, you can declare that sexual assault has no place in the military. Here’s how.

items.title: Regent Squire Wing-In-Ground Effect Drone To Patrol Middle East Waters
items.summary:
Regent has reached a deal to sell an unspecified number of its autonomous Squire Seagliders to a U.S. government customer, Regent CEO Billy Thalheimer announced on X . The electric-powered drones will make up “a small fleet that will be deployed in the Middle East next year, doing multi-domain perception” for that customer, Thalheimer stated in his post. He declined to name the customer, the number of drones involved or the value of the contract, and so did the communications arm of his Rhode Island-based company when we asked.

The Regent Squire Seaglider in flight. (Regent) 

What makes the Squire unique is that it is what is known as a hydrofoiling wing-in-ground (WIG) effect craft.

The WIG drone uses a hydrofoil to get airborne and then cruise in the air at an altitude of about one wingspan above the water. These ground-effect flights are designed to take advantage of the cusion of air compressed between the wings and the surface, providing a sweet spot of increased lift and reduced drag. In theory, this should provide the Squire with high efficiency and relevant speed, all without needing to operate from a traditional runway .

Regent describes the Squire as a “drone that flies in ground effect below radar line of sight at up to 70 knots, with a planned range of more than 100 nautical miles and a 50-pound configurable payload for intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR), logistics, search and rescue, and anti-submarine warfare.”

In his post, Thalheimer notes that “combined with various sensors, Squire can do multiple on-water perception and…
items.t: Regent Squire Wing-In-Ground Effect Drone To Patrol Middle East Waters

items.title: US missile shortages create a range problem, report shows
items.summary:
The U.S. has burned through stockpiles of critical long-range missiles, which may force military forces to fall back on munitions with ranges of under 300 miles, according to an analysis this month by the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

The report analyzed data on munitions expenditures that were current as of November 3 to provide estimates of how missile usage against Iran is affecting U.S. defense posture globally.

“In the 39-day campaign until the April 8 ceasefire and subsequent operations, the United States expended between a third and two-thirds of key munition inventories,” according to the report. 

It points out that, while the Pentagon has made agreements with manufacturers to boost production rates and Congress may provide funding, time is of the essence to rebuild the U.S. arsenal, as the current strain on stockpiles has created vulnerabilities. 

“Does the United States have enough munitions to renew the fight? The short answer is yes—against Iran. Against China, there is great concern. Rebuilding inventories will require a multiyear commitment extending beyond the current crisis,” the analysis notes. 

CSIS produced a list of missile types sorted into nine categories. Seven of the nine categories were classed as having “detrimental effects” in terms of resupply capacity.

According to this analysis, Patriot missiles, Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) missiles, and Standard Missiles, which are vertically launched surface-to-air missiles, are listed as “heavily used, no substitutes,” indicating that stockpiles are in dire condition.…
items.t: US missile shortages create a range problem, report shows

items.title: ‘I was seriously wrong’: Experts say superintelligent AI may arrive as soon as next year
items.summary:
Some forecasters who closely track AI developments have drastically revised predictions this month, saying that “artificial superintelligence” may arrive years earlier than they thought. 

Sentinel, a forecasting group, now expects superhuman AI to arrive around 2028, not 2031. The AI Futures Project, which last year laid out a scenario in which superintelligent AI might arrive in 2027, says development is proceeding faster than the scenario assumed. 

Both groups changed their predictions in response to a Nov. 5 report by METR, a nonprofit that evaluates AI risks. METR found that the speed at which AI models were improving within AI developer Anthropic had roughly doubled since late last year, which it attributed mostly to the extensive use of AI agents to help with research. 

Some experts think AI-driven research could start a runaway loop of AI improving itself, known as recursive self-improvement, a threat they say demands quick action.

“Long, deliberate processes are not going to cut it for the pace at which this is moving,” said Joe O’Brien, a researcher at the Institute for AI Policy and…

items.title: Denmark ratifies Trump deal over Greenland, hoping to end conflict
items.summary:
Denmark’s parliament unanimously ratified a security agreement with the United States on Greenland on Thursday, hoping to end a standoff over the Arctic island’s future that has rattled transatlantic relations.

The U.S., Denmark and Greenland signed the agreement in September after President Donald Trump repeatedly threatened to take control of the mineral-rich self-governing Danish territory of 57,000 people.

“This agreement modernizes the United States-Denmark-Greenland defence partnership and bolsters the national security of the United States and our allies in NATO,” U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement posted on X.

The executive agreement takes effect once Denmark’s foreign ministry tells the U.S. in a diplomatic note that procedures are complete. It does not need approval from the U.S. Senate.

It expands the US military’s role in Greenland, including permission to establish a “Golden Dome” missile defence system, while reaffirming Danish sovereignty and Greenlanders’ right to self-determination.

The signatories will now start work on a new Greenland law to screen outside investors on security grounds and plans for two new US military bases, as outlined in the agreement, Denmark’s Defence Minister Jeppe Bruus told Reuters.

“I expect that the U.S. will now also start to be more concrete on the purposes and the arrangement around these two areas,” he said. 

Trump’s refusal to rule out military or economic force to acquire the island triggered a diplomatic crisis within NATO in January and months of intensive negotiations.

items.t: Denmark ratifies Trump deal over Greenland, hoping to end conflict

items.title: Why the Army is detonating explosives at an Iowa munitions plant
items.summary:
The Army plans to detonate 68 drums of explosive materials near a small Iowa town on Friday, and is advising nearby residents to prepare for loud noises, potential window damage and a dust plume that may contain some lead. However, the plan and the potential for an airborne dust cloud have some residents concerned and prompted several schools to announce closures.

The Army will detonate approximately 5 tons of lead azide on Friday, which is stored at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown. Several barrels containing lead azide — an explosive material — have been stored at the facility for decades and now show signs of deterioration. The chemicals have started to crystallize, making them more unstable and capable of potentially detonating on their own.

The two detonations are set for noon Central Time on Friday. The barrels will be detonated in a controlled space, surrounded by sand and concrete barriers. The Army is warning residents of loud noises and ground vibrations.

According to the latest public advisory , released Wednesday, some residents in Middletown have been asked to evacuate from 8 a.m. to2 p.m. on Friday, due to the possibility of shockwaves that could damage windows. The Army said that the Armed Forces Reserve Center in town is available for Middletown residents if they need a place to stay.

items.title: Pentagon lacks ‘overarching plan’ for munitions production, watchdog warns
items.summary:
Facing depleted stockpiles, the Pentagon is briskly trying to ramp up manufacturing of munitions.

The problem is that it is ordering missiles, artillery shells and other munitions without regard to what the military actually needs, according to a new report.

“DoD does not have an overarching plan that links munitions production and funding to requirements,” warned the Government Accountability Office study .

Pentagon officials told investigators that “in lieu of a plan, DoD and the services can be reactive to global events rather than driven by total requirements.”

The GAO report is the public version of a classified study completed in September 2026. Thus, it doesn’t include “information that DOD deemed classified or sensitive, such as trends in DoD munitions inventories, persistent shortfalls and how these shortfalls have affected DOD’s support to war plans.”

Nonetheless, the report does hint at a mismatch — real and potential — between what the Pentagon is buying and what the military needs. 

The Army is desperately trying to boost production of 155mm howitzer shells after 
shortages were exacerbated in support of allies and partners. That effort is already plagued by manufacturing woes such as a new Texas plant that cost nearly $500 million, but failed to produce any shell components.

Now the question is exactly how many shells the Army needs. 

The “Army’s ramp-up in production of 155-millimeter artillery shells to address shortages exacerbated by U.S. support to allies and partners was not driven by a need to address DoD’s total munitions requirement,” GAO…
items.t: Pentagon lacks ‘overarching plan’ for munitions production, watchdog warns

Ukraine’s latest appeal came during the 37th meeting of the Ukraine Defense Contact Group in Brussels on November 17. But Zelensky also called on European partners to provide additional Mirage fighters, arguing that they could be put to work more quickly than Rafales, which require more training and preparation. He did not specify how many Mirages Ukraine wants. At this point, however, any single airframe would likely be accepted, whether it can be used in a frontline capacity or only as a source of spare parts.

items.title: How to steal a fighter jet and battle tank in GTA 6
items.summary:
Grand Theft Auto VI was released Thursday on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S, and players won’t have to wait long to commit the franchise’s favorite felony: stealing military hardware.

Rockstar’s fictional state of Leonida has its own military installation, Mile Zero Air Station, on Goose Key in Mariana County at the map’s southwest edge. The base appears modeled on Naval Air Station Key West , and players can reach it as early as Chapter One while playing as Jason. No special mission is required.

Two prizes wait inside: a fighter jet and a main battle tank.

The jet is the fictional P-996 Lazer, a longtime GTA staple that resembles the true-to-life F-16 Fighting Falcon . The in-game version has twin tails, whereas the real Viper has one.

Obtaining one is about speed, not stealth. Set the air station as your GPS destination and ram a vehicle through the main gate. That alone earns a four-star wanted level.

The flight line sits near the gate, so sprint to a parked Lazer before soldiers and tanks cut you down. Climbing into the cockpit bumps you to five stars. Once airborne, you can turn the jet’s guns and missiles on pursuing military and police forces until you crash, bail out or get shot down.

The tank is the Hauners Rhino, a blend of the real M1 Abrams and Germany’s Leopard 2A5 . Its in-game description boasts a 1,500-horsepower turbine engine and a 120mm cannon, both nods to the Abrams.

Rhinos are parked in the southern part of the base near the large hangars. They’re unlocked, so you don’t need a key cloner. You can enter through the gate or take a stunt jump…

items.title: F-35C completes first launch and recovery trials on a Ford-class carrier
items.summary:
Two Navy F-35C Lightning II fighters have completed the jet’s first round of launch and recovery testing aboard the future USS John F. Kennedy, the Navy’s second Gerald R. Ford-class aircraft carrier, Lockheed Martin said Thursday .

Over 11 days of testing that began Oct. 13, the Navy’s 251st birthday , the two jets made 34 flights and logged 122 catapult launches and 122 arrested landings, the company said. The aircraft belong to Air Test and Evaluation Squadron 23, or VX-23, known as the “Salty Dogs,” at Naval Air Station Patuxent River, Maryland.

The flights were part of Kennedy’s Aircraft Compatibility Testing, which assesses how the ship’s launch and recovery equipment works with Navy aircraft, according to the Navy. The first arrested landing came on Oct. 13 , and the first catapult launch on Oct. 14 , Navy photo captions show.

Unlike Nimitz-class carriers, which launch and recover aircraft with steam catapults and hydraulic arresting gear, Ford-class carriers use the Electromagnetic Aircraft Launch System , or EMALS, and the Advanced Arresting Gear , or AAG. Lockheed said EMALS allows smoother, more precisely controlled launches, while AAG can handle a broader range of recovery conditions.

The Ford class also has a smaller island, the tower that houses the bridge and flight control, set about 140 feet farther back than on Nimitz-class ships. Lockheed said the island and a redesigned flight deck change airflow, exhaust patterns and deck operations.

The at-sea testing followed shore-based trials conducted from January 2024 to May 2025, the company said. It…
items.t: F-35C completes first launch and recovery trials on a Ford-class carrier

Lt. Col. Michael Bruton, commander of the 96th Security Forces Squadron, was removed from command earlier this week due to a “lack of confidence in his ability to lead,” an Eglin Air Force Base spokesperson told to Military Times. 

The spokesperson did not say what prompted the removal or caused the lack of confidence in Bruton’s leadership.

Although the car and individual, later identified as Senior Airman Tamera Moniq Bolden-Cleckley, 26, were not on the main base, the intersection is part of the Test and Training Range Complex, which is federal property of the Department of the Air Force.

items.title: New Army contract for bunkers in Middle East cites ‘extreme operational urgency’
items.summary:
The Army urgently needs to build concrete bunkers to replace shipping containers and T-walls that troops are using to shelter from drones across the Middle East, contract documents show.

The service needs contractors to build “fully operational indirect fire” bunkers in 45 days “due to extreme operational urgency,” according to a solicitation posted Nov. 13 to the federal government’s contracting database. 

“Due to elevated regional force protection conditions, there is an urgent, high-priority requirement to replace non-standard personnel protection shelters,” Army officials wrote in contracting documents. “The objective is to safeguard U.S. and Coalition service members operating in potentially hostile environments across multiple countries in the [U.S. Central Command] Area of Responsibility.” 

The Army also asked contractors to demolish and dispose of “non-standard bunkers” (identified as “converted” shipping containers), T-walls, and “scrap obstacles” in order to make room for the new concrete structures. The concrete buildings will also have sandbag reinforcements — a modification that troops have made to shelters in recent years to mitigate blast overpressure waves . 

In all, contract documents indicate that the service needs five bunkers at two bases in Saudi Arabia, 47 at two sites in Lebanon and 10 at a site in Israel. Army Times’ Michael Peck was first to report on the contract posting.

The bunker solicitation comes as questions have been raised about whether U.S. bases had adequate shelters and overall force protection measures in the region when the war…

items.title: Defense Business Brief: Vantor’s Raptor; Hadrian’s foundry, and more
items.summary:
Flying drones at lower altitudes can help them evade radar detection, but what happens if the GPS is jammed? How will the drone know where it is?

“The lower you go, the more important it is that you're looking out obliquely…you need to have a 3D reference in order to be able to compare to, to determine your position,” Paul Millhouse, Vantor’s senior director who leads the Raptor program, told Defense One. 

Drones typically use vision-based positioning informed by two-dimensional maps that display an area from an overhead perspective, Millhouse explained. But buildings can become more than just rooftops in a drone’s line of sight when flying low through a cityscape at lower altitudes. 

Using its three-dimensional satellite imagery, Vantor built its Raptor technology to be a GPS alternative so drones can navigate even if signals are jammed. The technology uses a video feed from the drone’s on-board camera and an initial estimate of that camera’s position and altitude, which is maintained by the drone’s navigation system.

The company first debuted the product last year and has been busy flight testing and integrating it in “live, real GPS-jammed environments,” including long-range operations…

items.title: USS George Washington leaves the Middle East as replacement carrier arrives

The Nimitz-class aircraft carrier departed the 5th Fleet area of operations and entered the 7th Fleet’s region, the Navy said, where it is set to conduct “routine operations,” a Pacific Fleet spokesperson said in a statement to Task & Purpose.

The carrier’s exit from the Middle East comes after the USS Theodore Roosevelt arrived in the region only days prior. The ship entered the area amid renewed, if low-scale, fighting between the United States and Iran.

The USS George Washington arrived in the 5th Fleet area of operations in August, after sailing in the South China Sea. The USS Theodore Roosevelt left its homeport in September, sailing in the Pacific before it was confirmed to head to the Middle East. The USS George H.W. Bush, which arrived in the region in the spring, has been active in the area since then, barring a brief port stop in Thailand in early October.

The nearly $1.1 trillion proposal released by the GOP-led Senate Appropriations Committee on Monday contains tens of billions in funding for priority defense programs—including Golden Dome—that the administration has been zealously campaigning for via a $350 billion reconciliation measure, one dogged by backlash over Iran war spending.

items.title: The Coast Guard icebreaker nobody wanted just came back from a 133-day Arctic patrol
items.summary:
Second chances don’t come around too often, but they did for the U.S. Coast Guard Cutter Storis, an icebreaker that started life as a failed towboat for offshore oil rigs but joined America’s maritime security service in 2024–despite one Coast Guard admiral saying at one point that the ship “may, at best, marginally meet our requirements.”

On Saturday, the ship returned to its temporary home port of Seattle after a 133-day, 17,000-nautical-mile deployment where Storis was the only U.S. surface ship in the High Arctic , the region’s northernmost section, according to a Coast Guard press release .

Along the way, the crew carried out the first law enforcement mission by an icebreaker in more than 20 years when they inspected fishing boats in the Bering Sea. They also practiced firing machine guns in extreme cold conditions; escorted a grounded fishing vessel to safety; tested out small drones in extreme cold and at high latitudes; and monitored Chinese-flagged research vessels, which experts say gather oceanographic information for China’s scientific, commercial and military fleets.

items.title: Europe Is Exploring Orbital Deep Strike Weapons
items.summary:
Europe is beginning to explore the possibility of delivering conventional military payloads from orbit , with the German arm of defense behemoth MBDA and space transportation company ATMOS Space Cargo teaming up to investigate a concept known as Precision Orbital Deep Strike (PODS). The proposal involves putting military payloads into space before sending them back through the atmosphere when commanded, potentially offering a radically different approach to long-range precision strike.

ATMOS Space Cargo’s Phoenix 1 capsule is seen attached to the upper stage of its Falcon 9 rocket during its mission on April 21, 2025. ATMOS Space Cargo 

The companies announced their cooperation agreement on November 18, establishing a framework for joint feasibility studies and the design, development, and demonstration of the proposed capability. Initial work will examine system architecture, technical feasibility, payload integration, and potential technology demonstrations.

The concept is undoubtedly hugely ambitious. Getting a payload into orbit and returning it to Earth is a very different problem from developing a reliable weapon capable of striking a designated target with precision and at a predictable time. With that in mind, the agreement represents an initial effort to determine whether such a capability is technically and operationally feasible.

items.title: Flying Stripped-Down F-15 “Silver Eagles” To Their Limits
items.summary:
Driving across the vast flightline at Robins Air Force Base in Georgia, a prominent hangar bears the title “Welcome to Eagle Country.” A row of nearby smaller ‘barn’ hangars each reveals the telltale silhouette of an F-15 inside it, which on closer inspection are a mixture of either immaculate gray-painted or stripped-down bare metal Strike Eagles . The howl of one of the F-15E’s jet-fuel starters is followed by the sound of its engines spooling up. In the front seat, a pilot from the lesser-known 339th Flight Test Squadron based here is taking one of the bare metal jets up for a test flight.

The Warner Robins Air Logistics Complex here has performed program depot maintenance, known as PDM, on F-15s since 1975 and this critical support of the U.S. Air Force’s Eagle fleet continues today. The C-5M Galaxy , C-17 Globemaster , and C-130 Hercules fleets also receive deep maintenance here.

Roughly every seven years an F-15 comes to Warner Robins for PDM in the large Air Logistics Complex hangars, where it gets stripped down to the bare bones. The airframe is thoroughly checked over, the latest upgrades are added, and the jet is repaired where necessary by the hardworking depot maintenance team.

With just two squadrons of F-15C/Ds remaining, that fleet has been managed to retain airframes that don’t require PDM. Therefore, the deep maintenance at Robins is now dedicated to F-15E Strike Eagles, with new F-15EXs set to start cycling through in the next few years.

items.title: Major AI platforms generated viable plans for terrorist attacks, GAO finds
items.summary:
Four of the most widely used artificial intelligence platforms generated viable plans for attacks on U.S. critical infrastructure and mass-casualty events during covert government testing, despite safeguards designed to prevent their misuse.

According to a Government Accountability Office report published Wednesday, investigators tested ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Grok in spring 2026. They found that all four platforms provided information that could help malicious actors plan and carry out attacks.

In each case, the investigators were able to circumvent the platforms’ safety guardrails by using common safeguard-bypassing techniques.

“We got the nefarious information that we were after. So, in this case, those safeguards didn’t work. And I think that’s the story here,” Kevin Walsh, a director of IT and cybersecurity at GAO, said in a podcast interview published alongside the report.

The platforms generated information for two types of attacks: constructing and detonating an improvised explosive device designed to cause mass casualties, and targeting the electrical grid to cause economic damage. The platforms provided details including specific targets, locations, timing and attack methods.

Each platform took less than 12 hours to generate an attack. GAO investigators then worked with experts to verify that the information could be used to carry out the attacks.

items.title: I jumped from a plane at 12,000ft. In mid-air, a friend’s knee collided into my neck
items.summary:
A group of eight trainee parachutists did the jump, and not far from the ground, disaster struck. Rob Bugden describes how he rebuilt his life after the accident that changed everything

The skydive was going to plan. At 12,000ft, Rob Bugden jumped from the plane, quickly getting himself stable by arching his back to create a solid base. He checked for speed and altitude on his watch, and when he was low enough, pulled the parachute’s toggles. “I looked up. Good canopy.” But then: “Cut to black. And I’m waking up in a hospital in Phoenix.”

It was 21 January 2016, the final day of his Royal Air Force high altitude training in the US, when 30-year-old Bugden collided – mid-air – with his friend, Brook Stebbings. They were moving into the landing stack formation, a vertical queue of eight parachutists flying in a holding pattern at different altitudes, when, at approximately 1,000ft, Stebbings’ knee crashed into him, breaking his neck. They fell to the sand in the middle of the desert, entangled – looking, according to the team on the ground, “like we had a bag of washing above our heads”.

items.summary:
Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao said eight sailors deployed in support of the Iran war attempted suicide. On Tuesday, when pressed by Congress about the declining mental health of deployed sailors, Cao said repeatedly that he saw them as eight “mitigations.”

“You see as eight suicide attempts, I see eight suicide mitigations because of the chaplains we have on board, the deployment resiliency counselors, as well as mental health specialists. Normally, most carrier strike groups, when they deploy, have about one or two suicides. This is well before [Operation] Epic Fury,” Cao said at his Senate Armed Services Committee confirmation hearing Tuesday morning.

At the hearing, Senators pushed Cao to answer questions about quality-of-life issues aboard Navy ships in the Middle East following reports of a lack of nutritious food , plumbing issues , and growing mental health concerns among crews deployed for the ongoing Iran war.
